title: SAMDEF
subtitle: Edge Computer Vision System & Satellite Imagery Detection Pipeline
description: A high-performance computer vision system built in Rust and CUDA for large-scale satellite imagery (GeoTIFF) processing. Features an asynchronous multi-stage GPU pipeline, spatial grid NMS for deduplication, and a native GPUI (Vulkan) GIS desktop viewer delivering 0.20s/km² inference throughput.

gallery.caption: Native GPUI GIS Desktop Viewer: Real-time multi-class vector detection (1,256 active targets) & live radar minimap
Instant Class Soloing: Isolating 469 building footprints with zero GPU texture re-uploads & synchronized radar blips
Industrial & Storage Depot Scene: Multi-class GeoTIFF overlays with 0.31 m/px GSD telemetry
1600% Sub-Pixel Magnification & Pinned Target Inspector HUD: Ground dimensions (8.6m x 7.7m) & WGS-84 coordinates
Target Detection Table & Filtering: Isolated heavy vehicle telemetry with one-click GeoJSON & CSV exports
One-Click Table Target Focus: Instant jump to highway vehicle detections (#2132) with live radar frustum tracking
Interactive Geodesic Haversine Ruler: Measuring true WGS-84 ground distance & forward azimuth (121.0 m | 243.7°)

fullDescription:
# THE PROBLEM

Processing high-resolution satellite imagery (typically 3,000×3,000 to 15,000×15,000 multi-spectral GeoTIFFs) presents several key technical challenges:

1. Host Memory Spikes on Large Rasters:
Attempting to read and decompress large multi-spectral GeoTIFFs directly into contiguous host memory can quickly consume tens of gigabytes of RAM, causing severe swap thrashing and out-of-memory errors.

2. GPU Idle Time in Sequential Pipelines:
In a sequential loop (read -> tile on CPU -> upload -> run inference -> parse), the GPU sits idle while waiting for disk I/O and CPU tensor conversions, resulting in low hardware utilization.

3. Duplicate & Cut-Off Detections Along Tile Seams:
Slicing large satellite rasters into smaller tiles bisects objects (such as vessels, aircraft, and large buildings) across tile seams. Without boundary overlap buffers and spatial deduplication, models produce duplicate and cut-off bounding boxes.

4. Preserving Real-World Earth Coordinates:
Standard detection models output local pixel coordinates (e.g., x=450, y=320). Operators and GIS analysts require exact geospatial coordinates (WGS84 Latitude/Longitude, DMS, and ground footprint metrics) for mapping and operational use.

5. Desktop Viewer GPU Memory Overhead:
Rendering ultra-high-resolution rasters (e.g. 3,433×2,642 GeoTIFFs) with thousands of interactive detections requires careful graphics pipeline design. Generating raster overlays per filter toggle consumed ~41 MB of heap per click and caused UI stutter.

6. Bandwidth Limits for Cloud Processing:
Uploading gigabyte-scale satellite rasters over slow network uplinks introduces severe latency and high bandwidth costs. The workflow requires reliable local, air-gapped on-premise execution.

# THE SOLUTION

SAMDEF (Satellite Multi-Class Detection & Geospatial Framework) is a local, air-gapped, high-throughput system built in Rust and CUDA. It handles raster ingestion, virtual tiling, GPU tensor inference, spatial deduplication, database persistence, and native GPU-accelerated GIS visualization locally on edge hardware.

## Core Architecture Highlights:
• Pipelined Execution: A decoupled 3-stage thread pipeline using bounded Crossbeam channels that overlaps CPU preprocessing, GPU tensor inference, and async disk/network I/O to sustain 85–95% GPU core utilization.
• Virtual Tiling: Reads raster blocks directly via GDAL C-bindings in 896×896 windows with 20% stride overlap, keeping host memory strictly bounded.
• Geodetic Affine Projection: Maps localized pixel bounding boxes back into global geographic coordinates using GDAL 6-parameter GeoTIFF affine transform matrices.
• Spatial Grid NMS: Fast deduplication using spatial hash-buckets, eliminating tile-boundary duplicates efficiently.
• Native GPUI GIS Desktop Viewer (`gui_gpui`): A GPU-accelerated desktop application built with Rust and GPUI (Vulkan/Blade) delivering 5-layer immediate-mode rendering, sub-pixel cursor-invariant pan/zoom, class soloing, live radar minimap, geodesic Haversine ruler, target inspector HUD, tabular detection drawer, and GeoJSON/CSV/Markdown exports with zero GPU texture re-uploads.
• Binary Messaging Fabric: Uses Zenoh in peer-to-peer mode for low-overhead binary streaming between detection workers and database persistence.

# HIGH-LEVEL SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE


# SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE & DEEP DIVE

### 1. The Detector Microservice (`apps_deploy/detector`)
• Work-Stealing Producer Thread Pool (`modules/io/producer.rs`):
Scans the input directory for GeoTIFF files and spawns `PRODUCER_PARALLELISM` persistent worker threads. Each worker pulls image paths from a concurrent work queue, opens rasters using GDAL C-bindings, and slices them into fixed 896×896 RGB tiles with 20% stride overlap (179-pixel buffer) along horizontal and vertical axes.
• Decoupled 3-Stage Consumer Pipeline (`modules/io/consumer.rs`):
The consumer architecture is decoupled into 3 dedicated OS threads connected by bounded Crossbeam channels (`gpu_tx: bounded(4)`, `post_tx: bounded(64)`):
  - Stage 1 (OS Thread A - CPU Preprocessor & Batch Accumulator): Receives raw tile bytes from the input channel, bundles them into batches (optimal batch size = 2), and uses Rayon data parallelism (`par_iter`) across CPU cores to normalize pixels and transpose HWC to CHW planar format: normalized_val = (raw_byte / 255.0 - mean) / std. Ready `Array4<f16>` tensors are forwarded to the dedicated GPU channel in sub-milliseconds.
  - Stage 2 (OS Thread B - Dedicated GPU Inference Runner): A persistent OS thread holding the CUDA `Session` in ONNX Runtime (`ort` 2.0.0-rc.13) with native CUDA 13 support. Operates as a pure GPU execution loop without blocking file I/O. Dequeues ready tensors and immediately executes `session.run()` on the RTX 4060 GPU, forwarding raw output tensors to Stage 3.
  - Stage 3 (OS Thread C - Postprocessing, NMS & Tokio Async Output): Runs on the main Tokio runtime thread. Parses bounding box coordinates, shifts them by spatial tile offsets, tracks per-file completion in a HashMap, runs Spatial Grid NMS, and spawns background Tokio `JoinSet` tasks to write JSON and publish via Zenoh.
• Concurrency Advantage:
  - Thread A prepares Batch N+1 on CPU cores.
  - Thread B executes Batch N on the RTX 4060 GPU simultaneously.
  - Thread C saves Batch N-1 to disk and network simultaneously.
  - Bounded channels provide automatic backpressure: Thread 1 buffers up to 4 preprocessed batches in memory. When Thread 2 finishes a batch, the next tensor is pulled in 0 microseconds without waiting for CPU math. If CPU preprocessing outpaces GPU execution, `gpu_tx.send()` pauses Thread 1, preventing unbounded memory growth in RAM.
• Geodetic Affine Projection:
Every detected pixel coordinate is mathematically projected onto the Earth's surface using the GeoTIFF affine transformation matrix:
  X_geo = GeoTransform[0] + X_pixel * GeoTransform[1] + Y_pixel * GeoTransform[2]
  Y_geo = GeoTransform[3] + X_pixel * GeoTransform[4] + Y_pixel * GeoTransform[5]
• Spatial Grid NMS:
Standard Non-Maximum Suppression scales at O(N²), causing latency spikes when tens of thousands of detections occur across satellite scenes. SAMDEF partitions detections into spatial hash-grid buckets, restricting IoU evaluation strictly to adjacent spatial cells. Boundary duplicates are suppressed in sub-millisecond time.

### 2. Native GIS Desktop Viewer (`apps_deploy/gui_gpui`)
• Planar Configuration 2 & Chunky BGRA GeoTIFF Strip Decoder (`src/io/tiff_loader.rs`):
Satellite imagery frequently uses Planar Configuration 2 (separate color planes: RRR... GGG... BBB...) alongside interleaved RGB/RGBA/Grayscale strips. SAMDEF's custom decoder inspects TIFF header tags, streams separate strips across color planes, packs pixels directly into zero-copy BGRA8 memory wrapped in `gpui::RenderImage`, and simultaneously generates a downsampled BGRA thumbnail for the interactive radar minimap.
• 5-Layer Ordered GPU Scene Pipeline (`src/viewer/render.rs` & `src/viewer/overlays.rs`):
Built on GPUI's Vulkan/Blade immediate-mode compositor, the viewport separates primitives across five sequential `window.paint_layer` passes to guarantee strict z-ordering while preserving GPU instanced batching:
  - Layer 1 (`PolychromeSprite`): Renders the full-resolution GeoTIFF raster texture uploaded once to VRAM (plus optional luminance B/W inspection mode).
  - Layer 2 (`Quad` Batch): Instanced hollow neon vector bounding boxes (4 edge quads per visible target) with corner brackets on hovered/pinned targets and 100% transparent interiors.
  - Layer 3 & 4 (`Quad` + `MonochromeSprite`): Crisp GPU-shaped class and confidence glyph badges (`window.text_system().shape_line`).
  - Layer 5 (`PathBuilder` + `Quad` + `MonochromeSprite`): Interactive geodesic ruler line, crosshair endpoints, and metric telemetry pill.
  - Changing class filters, Solo isolation, or confidence thresholds triggers ZERO memory allocations and zero GPU texture re-uploads (< 0.1 ms).
• Sub-Pixel Cursor-Invariant Zoom & WGS-84 Geodesy (`src/viewer/state.rs` & `src/geo.rs`):
Implements smooth `exp()` scroll-wheel magnification (5% to 4000% plus `1:1` native pixel mode) anchored at the exact sub-pixel cursor coordinate. Projects cursor pixels via the GDAL 6-parameter affine matrix into live WGS-84 Decimal Degrees, Degrees-Minutes-Seconds (DMS), estimated Ground Sample Distance (`m/px`), target ground footprints (`m × m`, `m²`), and Haversine great-circle distance & forward azimuth (`0°–360°`).
• Inspection HUD, Detection Table & Multi-Format Exports (`src/ui/` & `src/io/exporter.rs`):
Features client-side Wayland/X11 window controls, instant dataset quick-search, an interactive radar minimap with neon target blips and draggable cyan viewport frustum, an occluded Target Inspector HUD card, a collapsible Target Detection Table with one-click target focus, and offline exporters for RFC 7946 GeoJSON (`FeatureCollection`), CSV spreadsheets, and Markdown summary reports.

### 3. Distributed Messaging & Database Processor (`apps_deploy/db_processor`)
• Zenoh Peer-to-Peer Bus (`modules/writer/zenoh_subscriber.rs`):
Subscribes to the topic pattern `satellite/detections/**`. Detection payloads published by the detector are deserialized from binary bincode into structured `DetectionPayload` objects.
• Persistent Geospatial Storage (`modules/writer/queries.rs`):
Connects to PostgreSQL using SQLx connection pooling. Converts pixel coordinates to WGS84 longitude/latitude via affine transforms and executes batched bulk inserts into `detections` (with PostGIS Point and Polygon geometry columns) and `detections_pixels` (with raw pixel coordinates), backed by spatial GIST indexing for rapid geospatial queries.

### 4. Training & Data Preparation Pipeline (`apps_training/`)
• Ingestor (`apps_training/ingestor`): High-throughput Rust microservice for automated dataset balancing, label format conversion, and GeoTIFF tile preparation.
• YOLO Model Trainer (`apps_training/yolo_model_trainer`): Python/PyTorch pipeline training YOLOv26s models on multi-spectral satellite imagery, featuring automated ONNX export with FP16 precision optimization.

# TESTING, VERIFICATION & BENCHMARKS

### Operational Inference Timing Benchmark (YOLO26s, FP16):
• Dataset: 281 high-resolution satellite scenes (~3,000×3,000 pixels each, 0.3m GSD)
• Total Geographic Area: 227.61 km²
• Hardware Testbed: Intel Core i9-13900HX (24 cores, 32 threads), 48 GB DDR5 RAM, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 (8 GB VRAM, CUDA 13)

title: SAMEX
subtitle: Cryptocurrency Spot Matching Engine & Distributed Trading Infrastructure
description: An event-driven spot cryptocurrency trading platform and order matching engine built with Turborepo, Bun, Apache Kafka, Redis, and Rust. Features an in-memory Central Limit Order Book (CLOB), exact integer accounting in cents, and real-time price streaming with <50ms end-to-end latency.
fullDescription:
# THE PROBLEM

Building reliable cryptocurrency trading backends and matching systems requires addressing several core concurrency, state, and accounting challenges:

1. Database Contention During High Order Volume:
Executing order matching directly inside relational database transactions causes lock contention, connection pool exhaustion, and latency spikes under load.

2. Floating-Point Rounding Drift:
Using standard IEEE-754 floating-point numbers for fractional asset balances introduces precision drift. Over millions of fills, tiny rounding discrepancies accumulate into ledger imbalances.

3. Opposite Position Handling in Spot Margin Trades:
In spot margin trading, if a user holding an open short position places a buy order, an engine must close the short first rather than mistakenly opening an opposing long position, which would create double-exposure risk and incorrect PnL.

4. Execution Timing & Stale Market Data:
Matching orders or evaluating liquidations against stale prices can cause inaccurate fills. Real-time mark prices and verified entry/closing prices must be maintained continuously.

5. Authentication Replays & Race Conditions:
OTP verification endpoints must prevent replay attacks and race conditions on concurrent verification requests.

6. Broadcasting Market Data at Scale:
Synchronously serving order book updates to thousands of web clients can saturate server I/O and degrade response times.

# THE SOLUTION

SAMEX is a microservices-based trading system organized as a Turborepo monorepo. It decouples trade ingestion, order matching, market data streaming, and persistence across services connected via Apache Kafka and Redis.

## Core Architecture Highlights:
• In-Memory Rust Matching Engine: A Central Limit Order Book (CLOB) using `BTreeMap` and FIFO ring buffers for sub-microsecond price-time priority matching with exact integer accounting in cents ($100,000.00 = 10,000,000 cents).
• Low-Latency Price Streaming: A Bun-powered WebSocket poller ingesting Backpack Exchange `bookTicker` feeds and publishing to Kafka, delivering updates to 1,000+ clients with <50ms end-to-end latency.
• Asynchronous Request-Response: Kafka topics handle user verification, balance checks, and trade persistence without blocking HTTP gateways.
• Atomic State Caching: Redis-backed OTP verification with atomic match-and-delete to prevent replay attacks, paired with fast session caching.
• Spot Margin & Position Closing: Settles open opposite positions before opening new exposure, with verified PnL accounting.

# HIGH-LEVEL SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                    SAMEX SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE                                    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

    ┌───────────────────────────────────┐               ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
    │      Next.js Web Trading App      │               │     External Exchange (Backpack)  │
    │  - Real-Time Trading Terminal     │               │  - Real-time bookTicker stream    │
    │  - Live Order Book & Charting     │               └─────────────────┬─────────────────┘
    └─────────────────┬─────────────────┘                                 │
                      │ (HTTP & WebSocket)                                │ (WebSocket)
                      ▼                                                   ▼
    ┌───────────────────────────────────┐               ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
    │       API Server (Express/TS)     │               │        Poller Microservice        │
    │  - WebSocket Broadcaster (Port 8080)              │  - Bun Runtime + WS Client        │
    │  - Auth & Trade Endpoints (3001)  │               │  - Zod Ticker Schema Validation   │
    │  - Redis Session & Price Cache    │               │  - Publishes to `price-updates`   │
    └─────────────────┬─────────────────┘               └─────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                      │ (Produce Requests)                                │ (Produce Tickers)
                      ▼                                                   ▼
    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                             APACHE KAFKA MESSAGE BROKER                               │
    │  Topics: user-requests | user-responses | price-updates | trade-requests | responses  │
    └─────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                      │ (Consume Trades)                                  │ (Consume User/DB)
                      ▼                                                   ▼
    ┌───────────────────────────────────┐               ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
    │      Rust Matching Engine         │               │     DB Processor (Bun + KafkaJS)  │
    │  - Central Limit Order Book (CLOB)│               │  - Async User Auth & Creation     │
    │  - Spot Margin & Position Logic   │               │  - Balance & Holdings Management  │
    │  - Realized PnL & Liquidation     │               │  - Prisma ORM + PostgreSQL        │
    │  - Integer Arithmetic (Cents)     │               │  - Completely Stateless & Scalable│
    └───────────────────────────────────┘               └───────────────────────────────────┘
```

# SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE & DEEP DIVE

### 1. In-Memory Rust Matching Engine (`apps/engine`)
• Central Limit Order Book (CLOB) Data Structures (`src/modules/order_matching.rs`):
Implemented in Rust using `BTreeMap<Price, VecDeque<Order>>` for bid and ask order ladders. Provides O(1) order insertion at existing price levels and O(log N) price tree traversal. Orders matching price criteria are executed strictly in FIFO sequence from ring buffers.
• Integer Accounting (Cents):
All asset prices, margin requirements, account balances, and order quantities are computed in integer cents ($68,452.18 = 6845218 cents, $100,000 = 10000000 cents). This eliminates floating-point epsilon inaccuracies and financial drift.
• Spot Margin & Opposite Position Resolution (`src/modules/execution.rs` & `pnl.rs`):
  - Position Invariant: Enforces that a user cannot hold both long and short positions simultaneously for the same asset.
  - Opposite Position Closure: When a user with an open short executes a buy order, the engine automatically detects the existing short position, matches against it, unlocks margin, and logs realized PnL based on `entry_price` and `close_price` in the `Trade` struct:
    Realized PnL (Short) = (Entry Price - Close Price) * Quantity
    Realized PnL (Long) = (Close Price - Entry Price) * Quantity
  - Only opens a new position if no opposite position exists or if residual quantity remains after complete closure.
• Deferred Trade Execution (`src/modules/processor.rs`):
When a trade request is consumed from Kafka, the engine stages the order and emits a balance inquiry to the DB processor. Matching only executes after the DB processor verifies adequate balance, preventing overdrafts.
• Real-Time Liquidation Engine (`src/modules/liquidations.rs`):
Continuously evaluates open position margins against incoming price ticks from the `price-updates` topic. If maintenance margin drops below threshold, liquidation triggers to protect exchange solvency.

### 2. Market Data Streaming (`apps/poller` & `apps/api-server`)
• Persistent WebSocket Ingestion (`apps/poller/src/index.ts`):
The Poller microservice (powered by Bun) maintains a resilient WebSocket connection to Backpack Exchange (`wss://ws.backpack.exchange/`), subscribing to real-time `bookTicker` feeds for SOL_USDC, BTC_USDC, ETH_USDC, DOGE_USDC, and BNB_USDC. Features automatic reconnection and rate limit backoff.
• Zod Schema Validation (`packages/schemas`):
Incoming payloads are validated before being published to the `price-updates` Kafka topic.
• WebSocket Broadcasting (`apps/api-server/src/index.ts`):
The API server consumes ticker updates from Kafka and broadcasts differentials to over 1,000 active WebSocket clients on port 8080.
• In-Memory Price Snapshots:
Concurrently updates latest prices in Redis with short TTLs for microsecond HTTP queries via `GET /api/v1/prices`.

### 3. Asynchronous Database Processor (`apps/db-processor`)
• Decoupled Kafka Consumer:
Built with Bun, KafkaJS, and Prisma ORM. Listens to `user-requests` (existence checks, user creation, credential validation, balance queries) and produces answers to `user-responses`.
• Complete Database Isolation:
Database operations execute asynchronously out-of-band, separated from HTTP gateways and matching engines.
• Horizontal Scalability:
Stateless architecture allows running multiple consumer replicas across Kafka consumer groups.

### 4. Security, Authentication & Session Handling
• Atomic Redis OTP Verification:
OTPs are hashed and stored in Redis with a 5-minute TTL. Verification executes as an atomic Redis transaction where matching and deletion occur in the same operation to prevent replay exploits.
• Credential Management:
Salted bcrypt password hashing with 12 salt rounds, and JWT session tokens delivered via httpOnly cookies.

# TESTING, VERIFICATION & BENCHMARKS

### 8-Payload Test Suite (`plans/payload_testing.md`):

```
Sequence of Verified Test Payloads:
1. User A places Buy Limit @ 11,000,000 (margin: 5000000, qty: 1.0) -> Added to book (Status: Open)
2. User B places Sell Market (margin: 5000000, qty: 1.0)           -> Matched @ 110k; User B opens SHORT
3. User B places Buy Limit @ 10,900,000 (margin: 5000000, qty: 1.0) -> Matched; closes User B SHORT (+100,000 PnL)
4. User A places Sell Market (margin: 5000000, qty: 1.0)           -> Matched @ 109k; closes User A LONG (-100,000 PnL)
5. User A places Buy Limit @ 12,000,000 (margin: 5000000, qty: 1.0) -> Added to book (Status: Open)
6. User B places Sell Market (margin: 5000000, qty: 1.0)           -> Matched @ 120k; User B opens SHORT
7. User B places Buy Limit @ 12,100,000 (margin: 5000000, qty: 1.0) -> Matched; closes User B SHORT (-100,000 PnL)
8. User A places Sell Market (margin: 5000000, qty: 1.0)           -> Matched @ 121k; closes User A LONG (+100,000 PnL)
```

### Verified Test Outcomes:
• User A: Completed two cycles (110k->109k, 120k->121k). Realized -$1,000 loss on cycle 1, +$1,000 profit on cycle 2. Margin unlocked, net balance 500,000 USD, 10 BTC.
• User B: Completed two cycles (110k->109k, 120k->121k). Realized +$1,000 profit on cycle 1, -$1,000 loss on cycle 2. Margin unlocked, net balance 500,000 USD, 10 BTC.
• Zero open positions remaining; zero orphaned contracts; margin released correctly.

### Spot Margin Profit/Loss Test Flow:
• Initial: User A and User B both start with 500,000 USD balance.
• Step 1: User A Buy 1 BTC @ 100,000 USD limit (10,000,000 cents); User B Sell 1 BTC @ 100,000 USD market.
• Step 2: User A Sell 1 BTC @ 101,000 USD limit (10,100,000 cents); User B Buy 1 BTC @ 101,000 USD market.
• Outcome: User A final balance = $501,000 USD (+$1,000 profit). User B final balance = $499,000 USD (-$1,000 loss). All margin unlocked.

### Performance & Latency Benchmarks:

| Operation / Subsystem | Measured Latency | Throughput / Capacity | Implementation Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market Data Streaming (E2E) | < 50 ms | 1,000+ WS clients | Backpack WS -> Poller -> Kafka -> API -> Web Client |
| User Signin (Auth) | ~200 ms | High-throughput | Kafka round-trip + bcrypt hashing (12 rounds) |
| Verify OTP & Account Create | ~270 ms | High-throughput | Kafka request-response + atomic Redis + PostgreSQL |
| Session & Profile (/me) | < 10 ms | 100,000+ ops/sec | Redis in-memory cache lookup |
| Kafka Message Broker | < 5 ms per hop | 10,000+ msg/sec | Dual-partition broker cluster with KafkaJS |
| Redis In-Memory Operations | < 1 ms | 100,000+ ops/sec | Session tokens, OTP with TTL, price cache |
| User Signup Flow | ~3.5 s | Scalable | SMTP email dispatch bottleneck (Gmail) |

title: WALPAY
subtitle: Digital Wallet Platform & Bank Webhook Service
description: A full-stack digital wallet and payment service built with Next.js 14, Node.js/Express, PostgreSQL, and Prisma ORM in a Turborepo monorepo. Features atomic transactions with database row-level locking, idempotent bank webhook handlers, P2P transfers, and wallet balance limits.

gallery.caption: Customer Wallet Dashboard: Balance breakdown, transfer interface, and transaction ledger

fullDescription:
# THE PROBLEM

In peer-to-peer digital wallets and payment processing systems, naive database updates and network retries create several common integrity challenges:

1. Concurrency Race Conditions & Double-Spending:
In high-concurrency payment systems, standard database update patterns (read balance -> check sufficiency -> deduct balance) allow critical race conditions. If a user initiates two simultaneous transfers of ₹5,000 with only ₹5,000 in their wallet, both parallel threads read the available balance before either write lock commits. Both transfers succeed, resulting in unauthorized double-spending.

2. Asynchronous Bank Reconciliation & Webhook Replays:
Banking networks communicate via asynchronous HTTP webhooks that frequently experience network drops, delayed callback deliveries, and automated retry storms. If a bank re-sends a deposit confirmation multiple times due to network latency, naive systems credit the user's wallet multiple times for a single bank deposit.

3. In-Transit Withdrawal Overdrafts:
When a user requests a withdrawal from their digital wallet to their external bank account, the settlement takes minutes to hours. If the wallet balance is not immediately locked in escrow, the user could transfer those same funds to another user via P2P before the bank processes the withdrawal, resulting in a negative balance.

4. Regulatory Compliance & Wallet Limits:
Financial regulations mandate strict balance ceilings (such as ₹1,00,000 maximum balance for standard KYC digital wallets). Payment systems must guarantee that no deposit or transfer can push an account balance beyond the statutory limit.

# THE SOLUTION

WalPay is a digital wallet platform built as a Turborepo monorepo. It features atomic transactions with row-level locking, a dedicated cryptographic bank webhook microservice with idempotency protection, a balance escrow state machine, and regulatory balance limit enforcement.

## Core Architecture Highlights:
• Row-Level Locking (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`): Implements pessimistic database locks within `prisma.$transaction()` blocks, preventing race conditions and double-spending during concurrent transfers.
• Dedicated Bank Webhook Engine: Express microservice validating inbound bank webhooks via secret headers (`x-webhook-secret`), duplicate idempotency tracking, and atomic status transitions (PENDING -> COMPLETED/FAILED).
• Fund Escrow State Machine: Automatically locks withdrawal amounts in a `locked` balance column during transit, preventing overdrafts while bank settlements clear.
• Regulatory Balance Capping: Programmatically enforces the ₹1,00,000 wallet limit across all deposit and transfer flows.
• Turborepo Structure: Organizes customer portal (`user-app`), landing site, and webhook microservice with shared database models (`@repo/db`), UI library (`@repo/ui`), and state management (`@repo/store`).

# SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE & DEEP DIVE

### 1. Concurrency Control & Row-Level Locking (`apps/user-app/app/lib/actions/p2pTransfer.ts`)
• Atomic P2P Transfers:
When a user initiates a P2P transfer, the operation executes within an atomic `prisma.$transaction()` block with pessimistic row-level locking via PostgreSQL:
```typescript
await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
    await tx.$queryRaw`SELECT * FROM "Balance" WHERE "userId" = ${Number(from)} FOR UPDATE`;

    const fromBalance = await tx.balance.findUnique({ where: { userId: Number(from) } });
    if (!fromBalance || fromBalance.amount < amount) throw new Error('Insufficient funds');

    const recipentBalance = await tx.balance.findUnique({ where: { userId: toUser.id } });
    if (recipentBalance && (recipentBalance.amount + amount > MAX_BALANCE)) {
        throw new Error('Recipient cannot receive money! Exceeds ₹1,00,000 regulatory wallet limit.');
    }

    await tx.balance.update({ where: { userId: Number(from) }, data: { amount: { decrement: amount } } });
    await tx.balance.update({ where: { userId: toUser.id }, data: { amount: { increment: amount } } });
    await tx.p2pTransfer.create({ data: { fromUserId: Number(from), toUserId: toUser.id, amount, timestamp: new Date() } });
});
```
• Lock Invariant:
The sender's balance row is locked at the database engine level. Any concurrent thread attempting to initiate a transfer or withdrawal on the same account is blocked until the transaction commits or aborts.
• Input Validation & Safety:
Validated via Zod schema (`transferSchema`): 10-digit phone number, positive amount, minimum ₹10 (1000 paisa), maximum ₹10,000 (1000000 paisa), and blocks self-transfers.

### 2. Bank Webhook Ingestion Engine (`apps/bank-webhook/src/index.ts`)
• Secret Header Verification:
All incoming bank callbacks verify the `x-webhook-secret` header against `process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET` before processing.
• Deposit Webhook Endpoint (`POST /hdfcWebhook`):
  - Receives payload: `{ token: string, user_identifier: string, amount: string }`.
  - Fetches the transaction by token. If `txn.status === 'Success'`, returns HTTP 200 with `Already processed` to handle bank retries idempotently.
  - Validates `txn.userId === Number(paymentInformation.user_identifier)` and `txn.amount === Number(paymentInformation.amount)`.
  - Executes atomic transaction: increments user balance and marks transaction `Success` with `endTime = new Date()`.
• Withdrawal Webhook Endpoint (`POST /hdfcWithdrawalWebhook`):
  - Receives payload: `{ token: string, status: 'SUCCESS' | 'FAILED', bankReferenceId: string, amount: number }`.
  - Verifies withdrawal token exists and has status `PENDING`.
  - Verifies amount matches expected withdrawal amount.
  - If bank status is `SUCCESS`: updates status to `COMPLETED` and decrements `locked` balance.
  - If bank status is `FAILED`: updates status to `FAILED`, unlocks amount from `locked` balance, and credits it back to available `amount` balance.

### 3. Balance Escrow & Regulatory Compliance
• Double-Entry Balance Ledger (`packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma`):
Tracks user balances in integer paisa using two distinct columns: `amount` (available funds) and `locked` (funds reserved in escrow). On withdrawal creation, funds move from `amount` to `locked`. Funds remain reserved in escrow until the bank webhook confirms final settlement, preventing in-transit overdrafts.
• Regulatory Balance Capping:
Programmatically enforces the ₹1,00,000 maximum wallet balance ceiling (`MAX_BALANCE = 10000000` paisa) across all deposit and transfer operations.

### 4. Monorepo Organization (Turborepo)
• `apps/user-app`: Next.js 14 application with authentication, transfers, withdrawals, transaction history, and p2p payments.
• `apps/landing-page`: Marketing and onboarding website.
• `apps/bank-webhook`: Standalone Express microservice for bank integration.
• `packages/db`: Centralized Prisma schemas, models, and migrations.
• `packages/ui`: Shared React component library.
• `packages/store`: Centralized state management atoms.
